rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited saying that each person is made ready for what they were created for does not establish the deterministic claim under discussion.
rows.anchor: فلا دلالة لها على ما ذكره أصلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deterministic argument makes divine decree render acts necessary and compelled, denying human choice and real causal links between acts and misery or felicity; it reduces those links to customary coincidence.
rows.anchor: توجب صيرورته ضروري الثبوت، ويكون الفعل بذلك مجبرا عليه لا اختياريا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An act's complete cause includes human will, sound tools, workable material, time and place, and the absence of obstacles; when all are present, the act necessarily occurs.
rows.anchor: فإن للعمل عله تامة يجب بها وجوده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An act is necessary relative to its complete cause but remains possible relative to each cause component, including human will; necessity relative to the whole does not turn the human relation into necessity.
rows.anchor: فللعمل إليها نسبة هي نسبة الوجوب، وله إلى كل واحد من أجزاء علته التامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human action remains voluntary even though a complete cause necessitates it; divine decree is an active attribute drawn from the ordered causal chain, and effects' necessity relative to their causes does not cancel human choice.
rows.anchor: ينتج أن الفعل اختياري للإنسان في عين أنه لا يخلو في وجوده عن علة تامة موجبة له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's knowledge that wood will burn by fire necessitates combustion conditioned on fire, not unconditioned combustion; likewise, knowledge of a chosen act or misery through disbelief entails its occurrence by choice, not independently of it.
rows.anchor: تعلق علمه تعالى مثلا بأن خشبة كذا ستحرق بالنار يوجب وجوب تحقق الاحتراق المقيد بالنار

rows.speaker: المجمع
rows.claim: Al-Majmaʿ glosses zafīr as the donkey's first bray and shahīq as its last bray.
rows.anchor: قال في المجمع الزفير أول نهاق الحمار والشهيق آخر نهاقه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī's al-Kashshāf defines zafīr as breathing out and shahīq as drawing the breath back in.
rows.anchor: وقال في الكشاف الزفير إخراج النفس والشهيق رده

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib defines zafīr as repeated breathing until the ribs swell; shahīq is prolonged zafīr and its return, while zafīr is its extension.
rows.anchor: وقال الراغب في المفردات، الزفير تردد النفس حتى ينتفخ الضلوع منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The senses are close, and the wording is metaphorical: the damned draw breath into their chests then expel it with loud crying and groaning from the fire's pain, like a braying donkey.
rows.anchor: والمعاني - كما ترى - متقاربة وكان في الكلام استعارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The collective context of the Day of Gathering favors plural wording; the preceding universal negation uses singular indefinite nafs, then the passage returns to the plural for the two groups.
rows.anchor: ومقتضاها المضي على هيئة الجمع الذين شقوا والذين سعدوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause describes the duration of Hell's inhabitants, just as the next verse describes the Garden's inhabitants, confirming their settled residence.
rows.anchor: بيان لمكث أهل النار فيها كما أن الآية التالية

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib defines khulūd as remaining unchanged and free from corruption; Arabs use it for things lasting a long time, even if mortal, then by extension for permanence.
rows.anchor: قال الراغب في المفردات الخلود هو تبري الشيء من اعتراض الفساد وبقاؤه على الحالة التي هو عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reported gloss takes the boys described as mukhalladūn to remain in their condition without corruption.
rows.anchor: قيل مبقون بحالتهم لا يعتريهم الفساد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second reported gloss understands mukhalladūn as wearing khulda earrings, with khulda being a kind of earring.
rows.anchor: وقيل مقرطون بخلدة، والخلدة ضرب من القرطة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāghib explains ikhlād as making something remain; in 7:176, a person who inclines to the earth is imagined to think he will remain there.
rows.anchor: وإخلاد الشيء جعله مبقى والحكم عليه بكونه مبقى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase reinforces permanence, yet worldly heavens and earth end while the Garden and Fire last forever; it also seems to measure post-Resurrection residence by a world that ends before it begins, the harder problem.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا يشكل الأمر في الآيتين من جهتين إحداهما تحديد الخلود المؤبد بمدة دوام السماوات والأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answer begins from Qur'anic mention of an afterlife earth and heavens unlike those of this world, removing the apparent time limit on everlasting residence.
rows.anchor: والذي يحسم الإشكال أنه تعالى يذكر في كلامه أن في الآخرة أرضا وسماوات وإن كانت غير ما في الدنيا بوجه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an describes an afterlife earth and heavens, the Garden's inhabitants inheriting the earth, and the righteous receiving the final home; all that is with God endures, so only this world's heavens and earth perish while the afterlife's persist.
rows.anchor: فللآخرة سماوات وأرض كما أن فيها جنة ونارا ولهما أهلا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī argues that the afterlife has heavens and earth, citing the earth's replacement and the Garden's inhabitants inheriting the earth.
rows.anchor: حيث قال والدليل على أن لها سماوات وأرضا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī also suggests that what supports and shades the Garden and Fire counts as their earth and heaven, whether a created sky or the Throne.
rows.anchor: ولأنه لا بد لأرض الآخرة مما تقلهم وتظلهم إما سماء يخلقها الله تعالى أو يظلهم العرش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects the support-and-shade argument as weak: it makes heavens and earth dependent on the Garden and Fire, reverses the verse's duration relation, and fails to explain plural heavens.
rows.anchor: وإن كان الوجه الذي أشار إليه ثانيا سخيفا لأنه إثبات للسماء والأرض من جهة الإضافة

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Al-Qāḍī objects that comparing Paradise and Hell's duration to afterlife heavens and earth cannot clarify the point for most people, who do not know those things endure.
rows.anchor: حيث قال وفيه نظر لأنه تشبيه بما لا يعرف أكثر الخلق وجوده ودوامه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author answers that God's speech reveals the eternity of both the afterlife and its heavens and earth, so one revealed truth may explain the duration of another even if one is less familiar.
rows.anchor: وجوابه أنا إنما عرفنا دوام الجنة والنار بأهلهما من كلامه تعالى كما عرفنا وجود سماوات وأرض لهما

rows.speaker: الآلوسي
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says the apparent sense is the familiar celestial bodies and recommends another explanation.
rows.anchor: أن المتبادر من السماوات والأرض هذه الأجرام المعهودة عندنا فالأولى أن يلتمس هناك وجه آخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author replies that language gives general concepts, while reflection and cross-reading determine their intended referents; the Qur'an interprets and confirms itself, so familiar worldly referents need not be imposed.
rows.anchor: وأما في مقاصدها وتشخيص المصاديق

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: The second view means the heavens and earth of Paradise and Hell: what is above and shades them is heaven, and what they rest on is earth.
rows.anchor: الوجه الثاني إن المراد سماوات الجنة والنار وأرضهما أي ما يظلهما وما يقلهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects that view because it does not explain why the verse uses plural heavens, and he has already shown its broader conceptual problem.
rows.anchor: على أن هذا الوجه لا يفي لبيان السبب في إيراد السماوات في الآية بلفظ الجمع

rows.speaker: مفسرون
rows.claim: A third view takes the phrase as a comparison: Paradise and Hell last as long as the afterlife, just as the worldly heavens and earth last for their own span.
rows.anchor: الوجه الثالث إن المراد ما دامت الآخرة وهي دائمة أبدا كما أن دوام السماء والأرض في الدنيا قدر مدة بقائها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If read as a simile, this third view implies termination contrary to the intended meaning; any other reading is unsupported by the wording.
rows.anchor: وفيه إنه لو أريد بذلك التشبيه كما ذكرناه أفاد خلاف المقصود أعني الانقطاع

rows.speaker: مفسرون
rows.claim: A fourth view treats the phrase as Arabic hyperbole for endless duration, like expressions that last as long as night and day differ or stars rise.
rows.anchor: الوجه الرابع إن المراد به التبعيد وإفادة الأبدية لا أن المراد به التحديد بمدة بقاء السماوات والأرض بعينها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects this usage for God, who explicitly teaches that the heavens and earth are appointed and perishable; their names cannot properly be used as a term for eternity in His speech.
rows.anchor: وأما من يصرح في كلامه بأنها مؤجلة الوجود منقطعة فانية ويعد الإيمان بذلك إحدى فرائض النفوس

rows.speaker: مفسرون
rows.claim: A fifth view gives the damned a finite span as long as the heavens and earth last, then an added endless duration, analogously to people remaining for epochs in 78:23.
rows.anchor: الوجه الخامس أن يكون المراد أنهم خالدون بمدة بقاء السماوات والأرض التي يعلم انقطاعها ثم يزيدهم الله سبحانه على ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects the fifth view because it assumes the phrase divides duration into a finite part and an infinite addition, a reading requiring unstated premises absent from the wording.
rows.anchor: وفيه إنه على الظاهر مبني على استفادة بعض المدة

rows.speaker: مفسرون
rows.claim: A sixth view identifies the Garden and Fire here with their Barzakh counterparts, which last until Resurrection, when their inhabitants leave for judgment.
rows.anchor: الوجه السادس إن المراد بالنار والجنة نار البرزخ وجنتها وهما خالدتان ما دامت السماوات والأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects the Barzakh view as contrary to the context, which describes Resurrection Day and its eternal reward and punishment; Barzakh punishment is exposure to the Fire, not entry into it.
rows.anchor: على أن الله سبحانه يذكر عذاب أهل البرزخ بالعرض على النار لا بدخول النار

rows.speaker: مفسرون
rows.claim: A seventh view reads entering Hell as entering Satan's authority, whose form becomes Fire, and dwelling in the Garden as God's authority, whose form becomes bliss; people may enter or leave either through changes in faith and conduct.
rows.anchor: الوجه السابع إن المراد بدخول النار الدخول في ولاية الشيطان وبالكون في الجنة الكون في ولاية الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says this is sound as an inward meaning but not the apparent one: the passage describes Resurrection's unique terrors to warn and reassure, not pre-Resurrection spiritual states hidden from its audience.
rows.anchor: نعم هو معنى صحيح في نفسه في باطن القرآن

rows.speaker: مجمع البيان
rows.claim: A second view in al-Majmaʿ al-Bayān treats the exception as additional punishment in Hell and added delight in the Garden beyond the stated measure, with illā meaning 'besides'.
rows.anchor: وثانيها أنه استثناء في الزيادة من العذاب لأهل النار والزيادة من النعيم لأهل الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects that view because it assumes 'as long as the heavens and earth' is not eternal, contrary to his earlier explanation.
rows.anchor: وفيه أنه مبني على عدم إفادة قوله

rows.speaker: مجمع البيان
rows.claim: A third view makes the exception cover time in the gathering and Barzakh before entry into Garden or Fire, to prevent readers thinking the afterlife begins immediately upon revelation or the end of obligation.
rows.anchor: وثالثها إن الاستثناء واقع على مقامهم في المحشر لأنهم ليسوا في جنة ولا نار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author finds no textual evidence for this view and says it seems to assume that misery and happiness are fated without human acquisition or choice, a reading already rejected.
rows.anchor: وفيه إنه لا دليل عليه من جهة اللفظ

rows.speaker: مجمع البيان
rows.claim: A fourth view attaches the Hell exception to kinds of torment beyond sighing and gasping, and the Garden exception to kinds of pleasure, inferred from its uncut gift.
rows.anchor: ورابعها إن الاستثناء الأول متصل بقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects the fourth view as an unsupported break in parallel context: 'uncut gift' establishes duration, not kinds of pleasure, and there is no cue for the proposed exception.
rows.anchor: وفيه إنه قطع لاتصال السياق ووحدته من غير دليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One parse makes mā a verbal noun, meaning 'unless your Lord wills their non-eternity'; the author weakens it because the following 'what He wills' uses mā as a relative pronoun with the same referent.
rows.anchor: و { ما } في قوله { ما شاء ربك } مصدرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, mā is a relative pronoun and the exception concerns duration: they remain for all future times except a span God wills.
rows.anchor: وإما موصولة والاستثناء من مدة البقاء المحكوم بالدوام الذي يستفاد من السياق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another relative-pronoun parse attaches the exception to the hidden plural subject of 'remaining': everyone stays except those God wills to remove from Hell and admit to the Garden.
rows.anchor: أو الاستثناء من ضمير الجمع المستتر في خالدين

rows.speaker: الأخبار
rows.claim: The author says this reading agrees with reports that sinful believers do not remain in Hell forever but eventually leave for the Garden through intercession.
rows.anchor: فيكون تصديقا لما في الأخبار أن المذنبين والعصاة من المؤمنين لا يدومون في النار بل يخرجون منها ويدخلون الجنة بالآخرة للشفاعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although uncommon, mā can refer to rational beings, as in the Qur'anic instruction to marry whichever women are pleasing.
rows.anchor: ويبقى الكلام في إيقاع { ما } في قوله { ما شاء } على من يعقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the Garden is an uncut gift, its exception signals God's continuing ability to expel its inhabitants, not an actual exit; He will not do so, keeping His promise and retaining unrestricted power and sovereignty.
rows.anchor: ولازمه أن لا يكون الاستثناء مشيرا إلى تحقق الوقوع فإنه لا يلائم كون الجنة عطاء غير مقطوع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The paired exceptions preserve God's absolute power: no gift or withholding binds Him or removes His ability to act otherwise; the Hell clause matches the Garden clause, and reports of some sinners leaving Hell remain compatible.
rows.anchor: فأهل الخلود في النار كأهل الخلود في الجنة لا يخرجون منها أبدا إلا أن يشاء الله سبحانه ذلك لأنه على كل شيء قدير
